facts.claim: Subtitle: Solving Problems and Selling Ideas with Pictures. Roam argues any problem can be made clearer with a picture, and any picture can be made with the same set of tools and rules.
In the introduction Roam notes kindergarteners draw freely while adults do not; adults have forgotten how to express themselves visually.
The book says visual thinking needs no artistic skill, only three tools everyone has: eyes (to look), mind's eye (to imagine) and hand-eye coordination (to draw and show).
Four steps of visual thinking: look, see, imagine, show (collecting and screening; selecting and clumping; seeing what is not there; making it clear).
Six ways of seeing map to six pictures: who/what to a portrait, how much to a chart, where to a map, when to a timeline, how to a flowchart, why to a multiple-variable plot.
SQVID: five pairs used when imagining an idea: simple vs elaborate, quality vs quantity, vision vs execution, individual attributes vs comparison, delta (change) vs status quo.
SQVID can be run in order to focus the idea, or each pair can be weighted toward what matters most to the audience (audience focusing).
Case study company in the book: SAX Inc., an accounting software company whose sales are stagnating as competitors gain ground.
Southwest Airlines origin: Rollin King, winding down a small regional carrier, talked the idea over with his lawyer Herb Kelleher: a small airline linking large Texas cities rather than small towns.

The sketch: a triangle with Dallas, Houston and San Antonio at its corners (three dots for the cities, three arrows for direct flights), drawn on a napkin, set against the tangled route maps of traditional hub-and-spoke airlines.

Roam uses the story to show that a simple picture made the airline easy to sell to investors and customers. Accounts differ on who held the pen (King or Kelleher). The Globe reviewer adds that the airline might have started without the napkin.
Part Three: begin from a blank napkin, draw the most important element in the middle; for a competitive landscape start with yourself, because you know you are there.

Outside the book: Wikipedia calls the cocktail-napkin story a founding myth; Kelleher and King both said there was no literal napkin. Kelleher was one of King's law clients; with banker John Parker they developed the Texas Triangle low-cost concept, modeled largely on California's Pacific Southwest Airlines.

Outside the book: Texas Co-op Power reports that not long before he died in June 2014 King said the napkin story wasn't entirely true, calling it a 'hell of a good story'. A bronze replica of the napkin sits at Southwest's headquarters at Dallas Love Field. The company was co-founded in March 1967 and first flew in June 1971.

Texas Co-op Power's telling places the legend in San Antonio in 1966, in a restaurant with a bar; the triangle has Dallas at the apex, San Antonio bottom left and Houston as the third corner; King was a pilot and businessman, Kelleher a lawyer.
